links.note: The tail question is whether Shruti will find the courage to speak to her father - the clash with his traditional views, answered from 'bite the bullet'; 733 would be the play's form, not this
Will the father attend the rehearsal - answered from his 'lost their sense of musicality' rejection, i.e. the traditional-versus-fusion conflict
Whether Shruti and her parents will come to understand one another - the generational reconciliation this theme is about
Identifying that the brackets hold stage directions and what they convey - reading the play's dramatic apparatus; 742 is for writing a script of one's own
How the bracketed directions help the actors - the function of stage directions inside the play, so 733 rather than the script-writing concept

The stem is a duplicate of the previous question (reported separately), but the stored item answers an extract on 'traditional values and modern expressions' and on 'lost' roots - squarely the generation-gap theme
The friends' differing attitudes to confronting parental authority - the youth side of the generational divide; the set has no character-analysis concept, and 733 covers only dramatic form
Naming the protagonist - a question in the vocabulary of dramatic structure about the play's central figure, where 734 is the conflict she is caught in
The band is Indo-Western fusion - the modern half of the fusion-versus-classical opposition
The father as a strict follower of Classical Hindustani music - the traditional half of the same opposition
Her terror is grounded in his view that Western tunes desecrate the violin - the artistic-values conflict itself
She will not hurt him because she respects him - the respect that makes the generational clash painful rather than simple defiance
The dinner as the moment she breaks the news - the confrontation scene of the conflict; 733 would be the act/scene division as such
Nabin realising she has not lost her classical roots - the resolution of the traditional-versus-modern clash
That she blends classical roots with new music beautifully - the synthesis this theme ends in
Leela opens Nabin's eyes - the bridging move between the generations
She reminds him of his own youth - the irony on which the generation-gap theme turns
The family's vocal-music heritage - the tradition Nabin himself once departed from
Nabin rebelled against his family's heritage - the previous generation's version of the same conflict
He rebelled to play a Western instrument - the repeated pattern across generations
He accepts his fears were baseless - the generational conflict dissolving
Diary entry in Shruti's voice about giving up the band for her father's wishes - the content is the generational clash; this set has no diary-writing concept, and 742 is script writing
Leela evaluated as a bridge between rigid tradition and modern aspiration - the generational divide stated in the question itself
Nabin's letter to his own late father reflecting on his rebellion and his daughter's - the theme across three generations
The message that embracing the new need not abandon the old - the resolution of 734, stated as the play's message
Why Nabin counts as a strict traditionalist - his view of musical purity and desecration, the traditional pole of the theme
Why she is terrified to reveal the fusion band - his classical strictness against her modern music
The friends' advice to 'bite the bullet' and speak openly about the band - advice about confronting the generational divide; the idiom itself is not a phrasal verb, so not 738
Her hesitation to hurt a father whose traditional values she respects - the tension inside the theme
When and how she breaks the news, including begging him to attend a rehearsal - the attempt to close the gap
Leela scolds her for the secrecy rather than the music - the mother's distinct position between the two generations
